A 63-year-old man visits his primary care physician for evaluation of a lung nodule that was incidentally
identified on a chest radiograph performed to rule out pneumonia. A CT scan confirmed the nodule to
be 8.5 mm in size. The patient is asymptomatic, has no history of smoking, and maintains an active
lifestyle, working at a dairy factory. His vital signs are normal, including a temperature of 97.6°F
(36.4°C), blood pressure of 127/80 mmHg, pulse of 78/min, respirations of 14/min, and oxygen
saturation of 98% on room air. Physical examination, including lung auscultation, is unremarkable.
What is the most appropriate next step in management? Answer Choices: (A) CT scan in 6 months (B)
Biopsy and lymph node dissection (C) Repeat chest X-ray in 3 months (D) PET scan (E) Surgical
resection of the nodule (F) Sputum cytology analysis (G) Antibiotic therapy for presumed infection (H)
Bronchoscopy with biopsy (I) No further workup indicated (J) CT-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy
 A. Bronchoscopy with biopsy
B. Repeat chest X-ray in 3 months
C. No further workup indicated

D. Biopsy and lymph node dissection
E. CT-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy
F. CT scan in 6 months
G. Antibiotic therapy for presumed infection
H. Surgical resection of the nodule
I. Sputum cytology analysis
J. PET scan
